description: Talavera Orbital is a team from Puebla, Mexico, led by Salvador Martínez Ayala, a Systems & IT Engineering student. I build end to end: Python data pipelines, Node.js/JavaScript web apps and simulations grounded in real NASA open data. Focus: rigorous analysis, clear visualizations and strong storytelling. Looking for teammates in Earth/space science, data visualization, UI/graphic design or video who want to aim for a Global Award. Español / English.
summary:
One calendar. Different sensors. Visible uncertainty.

Talavera Orbital is a free web app that puts NASA FIRMS hotspot detections from MODIS and VIIRS on one consistent monthly calendar, from the start of the MODIS record to today, for any area of Mexico and Argentina.

We convert every MODIS detection into VIIRS-equivalent detections with factors learned on the years both sensors overlap, separately by satellite clock, month, day/night and country, and we show each estimate with its uncertainty range.

We turned the challenge's own success criterion, "the sensor of origin no longer matters", into a single pre-registered test against the agreement between twin VIIRS satellites.

Result: In our held-out 2019–2021 test, harmonized MODIS did not meet the pre-specified criteria for interchangeable unusual-month classifications at the 3° block scale. The calendar remains useful for exploring historical hotspot detections, but its pre-2012 anomaly flags are indicative rather than validated.

What we had seen of 2019–2025 data before the test (prior exposure) and a post-freeze addendum are stated in full in the Validation section of the Detailed Project Description.

It is built for historical analysis, research and planning, not for real-time tactical response.
details:
Detailed Project Description

What it does

  • Shows a year × month calendar of hotspot activity in VIIRS-equivalent hotspot detections for an area the user draws or types, in Mexico or Argentina, from the start of the MODIS record to today.
  • Marks every month as observed (VIIRS), estimated (MODIS converted, with an uncertainty range) or provisional (near-real-time data that FIRMS later replaces).
  • Flags each month as unusual, possibly unusual or typical against the same calendar month in the base years, and names the critical season of the area.
  • Compares the current month, to date, with the historical median of the same month.
  • Lets the user switch between "Vegetation fires only" and "All thermal anomalies", so volcanoes such as Popocatépetl and industrial sources stop looking like wildfire activity.
  • Downloads a CSV whose rows match the count shown, plus a PNG of the calendar.
  • Labels every pre-2012 estimate "indicative": the single test did not pass in either country, so no area is labeled "reliable".

How it works

  • Data: NASA FIRMS standard-processing detections from the yearly country summaries, plus the FIRMS Area API for the current year; near-real-time months are labeled provisional.
  • One series, by era: Terra only, then Terra+Aqua (MODIS, converted), then Suomi NPP and NOAA-20 (VIIRS, observed).
  • Satellite clocks: Terra passes in the morning and Aqua in the afternoon, so each clock gets its own conversion factor by month, day/night and country, plus a shrunken local multiplier; on outage days the remaining platform is used alone.
  • Calibration: only on the MODIS–VIIRS overlap before the MODIS orbits drifted (Feb 2012 – Dec 2018).
  • Mask: one static mask of volcano and industrial heat sources, built from VIIRS standard data and applied identically to every sensor and to near-real-time data (which carries no source type).
  • Area of interest: your area snaps to the 0.1° grid: the cells whose center is inside it are used, and the snapped area is the one shown, counted and downloaded. Along coasts and borders, a cell counts as covered if its center is inside the country or the border crosses it; it only holds detections inside the country.
  • App: a static site (no server, no login) that reads precomputed tiles, so the CSV matches the calendar by construction.

Validation & uncertainty

  • Pre-registered, single run: the test design, thresholds and code were frozen and tagged (prereg-v1) before the run, and the test was run once on 2019–2021, three fire seasons held out from calibration.
  • Sensor-swap vs twin-swap: we compare how much the unusual-month flags change when NOAA-20 VIIRS is replaced by harmonized MODIS with how much they change when NOAA-20 is replaced by its twin, Suomi NPP, at the 3° block scale (~300 km).
  • Baseline and controls: a single overall count ratio per country (baseline M1) and no harmonization (control M0, which should fail). Uncertainty: 80 % ranges from leave-one-year-out residuals; 95 % intervals by bootstrap over 3° block × year.
  • Verdict rule: a country passes if P2, P3 and P4 all pass at the 3° block scale. Neither country passed, so the pre-registered text C applies. Both splice checks passed, so the tested model is the published one.

Result (pre-registered text, verbatim): In our held-out 2019–2021 test, harmonized MODIS did not meet the pre-specified criteria for interchangeable unusual-month classifications at the 3° block scale. The calendar remains useful for exploring historical hotspot detections, but its pre-2012 anomaly flags are indicative rather than validated.

Prior exposure (pre-registration §2, verbatim): Before the test, we had inspected aggregate diagnostics that include 2019–2025 for Terra, Aqua and the VIIRS satellites: country-level annual counts and ratios, the yearly median overpass time, a country-level monthly calendar of raw detections for Mexico (2000–2025), and 2013–2024 pooled monthly, day/night, FRP-threshold and 1°-cell ratio distributions (H0/H2 QA); the NOAA-20 series itself, which the app displays from April 2018 onward, was visible at full resolution throughout development. No cell-month or block-month comparison of harmonized MODIS against VIIRS for 2019 or later was computed before the frozen run.

Addendum (identified after the freeze): the prior-exposure statement above omits further quality-control tables we had also seen before the test: (1) type-0 detection counts for Terra, Aqua and S-NPP by calendar month, pooled over 2013–2024, in two approximate boxes (Puebla, Mexico, and south-western Pampas including Bahía Blanca, Argentina); (2) counts of detections within 5 km of the Popocatépetl crater by platform and source type, with first and last year, up to 2025; (3) the yearly median and 90th-percentile MODIS pixel size, 2000–2025, for each country; (4) whole-record (2000–2025) country-level detection counts by platform, file version, source type and confidence class. None of them compares harmonized MODIS with VIIRS. The pre-registration was not changed.

Results by country (3° block × month unless stated; 95 % intervals in parentheses; published model E1c, both splice checks passed):

  • P2 · same unusual months. Cohen's κ, NOAA-20 vs harmonized MODIS (cross), compared with NOAA-20 vs Suomi NPP (twins). Pass: cross κ ≥ 0.60 and cross/twin ratio ≥ 0.75
    Mexico: fail · cross κ 0.51 (0.46–0.57) vs twins 0.75 (0.71–0.79); ratio 0.68 (0.61–0.75).
    Argentina: fail · cross κ 0.59 (0.53–0.65) vs twins 0.80 (0.76–0.84); ratio 0.74 (0.66–0.80).
  • P2b · three-state flag (decides the "reliable" label). Pass: "unusual" precision ≥ 0.80, "typical" precision ≥ 0.95, 80 % coverage 0.75–0.85, "possibly unusual" ≤ 50 %
    Mexico: fail · 67 % "possibly unusual"; "unusual" precision 0.69.
    Argentina: fail · 52 % "possibly unusual".
  • P3 · honest 80 % ranges, 1° cell × month. Pass: coverage 0.75–0.85 on cell-months with a non-zero estimate
    Mexico: pass · 0.80 (0.78–0.82), n = 4,545; including zero estimates 0.85 (0.83–0.86), n = 5,868; 1,323 zero-estimate cell-months left out.
    Argentina: pass · 0.79 (0.78–0.81), n = 5,153; including zero estimates 0.83 (0.81–0.85), n = 6,300; 1,147 left out.
  • P4 · better than the baseline, 1° cell × month. Skill = 1 − error of method / error of baseline. Pass: lower 95 % bound > 0
    Mexico: pass · skill 0.08 (0.05–0.12).
    Argentina: fail · skill 0.01 (−0.02 to 0.06).
  • J1 / J2 · Jul 2002 and Apr 2018 splices
    Mexico: pass / pass.
    Argentina: pass / pass.
  • P5 · Terra-only era (Dec 2000 – Jun 2002), same rules as P2, P2b and P3
    Mexico: fail · cross κ 0.41 (0.35–0.47), ratio 0.55; P3 passes.
    Argentina: fail · cross κ 0.40 (0.33–0.47), ratio 0.50; P3 passes.
  • Transfer into this country from the other one. T1 = all factors; T2 = shape only, level from the target country. Pass: |log B| ≤ 0.10, G ≤ 1.15, Δκ ≥ −0.05 (point estimates)
    Mexico: T1 fail · T2 pass.
    Argentina: T1 fail · T2 fail.
  • What this means: in Mexico the harmonized level beats the baseline and in both countries the 80 % ranges hold their coverage, but which months look unusual still depends on the sensor at the 3° block scale. Against the baseline, harmonization changed the unusual-month agreement only a little (cross κ 0.51 vs 0.48 in Mexico, 0.59 vs 0.54 in Argentina); the unharmonized control scored 0.03 and 0.14.
  • Transfer: one calibration does not serve both countries: full transfer (T1) failed in both directions, and transferring only the shape (T2) worked from Argentina to Mexico but not from Mexico to Argentina. Calibration should stay regional.
  • Labels in the app: "reliable" requires an area of at least one 3° block in a country that passed P2 and P2b. Neither country did, so after the test no area is "reliable". In Argentina, the class of areas with 30–100 MODIS detections per month passed P2 and P2b on its own, but the country-level failure keeps those areas "indicative".
  • Against our pre-registered expectation: we expected both countries to probably fail P2 and the method to beat the baseline in Mexico but not in Argentina, as happened; we also expected the 80 % ranges to cover NOAA-20 less often than Suomi NPP, which did not happen (on all cell-months, coverage against NOAA-20 was not lower than against Suomi NPP in either country).
  • VIIRS data gaps: a 2019–2021 month is excluded from every test if Terra, Aqua, NOAA-20 or Suomi NPP has 3 or more days without data in the FIRMS standard missing-data tables; the query of 2026-11-15 19:51:09 UTC listed no such day, so no month was excluded.
  • Trends: raw trends are descriptive only, shown with and without harmonization and labeled "Not comparable across 2012".

Limitations

  • Units are hotspot detections, not fires; one fire can produce many detections or none, and zero detections is not zero fire.
  • Pre-2012 unusual-month flags are indicative, not validated: in the single test they did not agree with VIIRS as closely as our pre-specified criteria required, in either country.
  • In Argentina, P2 failed on the point estimates, which is how the pre-registration decides (cross κ 0.59 vs the 0.60 threshold; ratio 0.74 vs 0.75); the 95 % intervals contain both thresholds (κ 0.53–0.65; ratio 0.66–0.80). We apply the pre-registered rule as written.
  • Months before VIIRS are estimates; applying the factors to earlier years assumes the overlap relation held then, checked only by internal consistency (the Jul 2002 splice check).
  • Level bias depends on activity. In a development check (calibrated on 2012–2015 and compared with S-NPP in 2016–2018; run EXP-002, not the held-out test), for the third of 1° cell-months with the lowest harmonized estimates the observed VIIRS counts were about 1.3–1.5 times the estimate, and for the third with the highest estimates the estimate was too high by up to about 5 %. This pattern is consistent with regression toward the mean when an estimate rests on few MODIS detections; it was not seen in country-level monthly totals, and we did not recalibrate for it. Read low-activity months before 2012 as probably too low, and very active months as possibly slightly high.
  • The Terra-only months (Dec 2000 – Jun 2002) are labeled indicative whatever the test says; their own check (P5) also failed.
  • "Reliable" requires an area of at least one 3° block in a country that passed the pre-registered unusual-month agreement tests (P2 and P2b). Neither country passed, so no area is "reliable"; the Puebla/Popocatépetl and Paraná Delta demonstration areas would stay "indicative" in any case, because they are smaller than one block.
  • The area of interest is a spatial approximation on the 0.1° grid (cells whose center is inside the area); along coasts and borders, covered cells are used whole but only hold detections inside the country.
  • In Argentina the mask catches only part of the MODIS detections that FIRMS classes as non-vegetation (volcano, other static or offshore sources): about half in 2000–2011 (Terra 52 %, Aqua 47 %), when the calendar uses MODIS, and 6–17 % per year from 2018, after FIRMS typing changed with the MODIS file version (11–14 % in 2017–2018), so some industrial heat can remain in the Argentine MODIS series.
  • In the Bahía Blanca preset area, the harmonized estimates for 2001–2003 are about 5–7 times the 2004–2011 average (7.1×, 5.6× and 5.0×); Terra's own raw detections there were 4.4–6.7 times its 2004–2011 average, so the jump is already in the MODIS detections, not created by the conversion. We did not recalibrate for it; read that early period with caution. The Puebla/Popocatépetl preset shows no such jump (2001–2003 about 1.0× its 2004–2011 average).
  • 26 MODIS platform-days (13 Terra, 13 Aqua, Jul 2002 – Apr 2017) are treated as missing because our data rule flagged them; 19 of the 26 are also listed in the FIRMS missing-data table, 7 are not.
  • The FIRMS missing-data table lists 9 Terra days in March and April 2002 (Terra-only period) that our availability table does not flag, so those two months are not marked incomplete and may be undercounted.
  • VIIRS data gaps: the rule above (Terra, Aqua, NOAA-20 or Suomi NPP with 3 or more missing days) excluded no month in 2019–2021.
  • The test years come from a different MODIS file version than the early product years; we checked for a step at the version change in 2016–2018 and the test did not detect one.
  • The test covers three fire seasons (2019–2021) in two countries.
  • Coverage is Mexico and Argentina; outside the processed area the app says so.
  • Not a real-time tool: the LANCE disclaimer states that, given their spatial resolution, the use of these data "for tactical decision-making or informing about conditions at a local scale are not advised". Talavera Orbital is for historical analysis, research and planning.

Challenge coverage

  • RT-01 Public web app, no login: Static site on GitHub Pages
  • RT-02 Harmonized MODIS + VIIRS series, reproducible: VIIRS-equivalent series; one command rebuilds it
  • RT-03 Activity calendar from the early 2000s to today: Year × month calendar
  • RT-04 Historical patterns, unusual conditions, critical periods: Unusual flags and critical season
  • RT-05 "The sensor of origin no longer matters": Turned into a pre-registered test, run once; it did not pass at the 3° block scale, and the app labels pre-2012 flags accordingly
  • RT-06 Resolution, sensitivity, overpass time: Treated by clocks, day/night and calibration; declared in Limitations
  • RT-07 Region and date range; downloads: Map + latitude/longitude fields with limits; CSV and PNG
  • RT-08 Busiest months and years; present vs past: Calendar ranking and current-month view
  • RT-09 Current month vs historical median: Month-to-date vs median of the same month
  • RT-10 Accessible color ramps: Colorblind-safe ramps: cividis (sequential, log scale) for counts and ColorBrewer RdBu (diverging, centered on the median) for anomalies; no rainbow, and every state also has a pattern, border style or letter, so nothing depends on color alone
  • RT-11 CSV matching what is shown: Rows = count shown, by construction
  • RT-12 Draw the area or enter coordinates: Rectangle drawing and coordinate fields
  • RT-13 Anomalies vs multi-year averages; detections reported: Anomaly view; raw detections by sensor plus harmonized value
  • RT-14 Users: emergency managers, brigades, scientists: For historical analysis, research and planning
  • RT-15 FIRMS cited with short name, version and DOI: NASA Data field below

Benefits & who it is for

  • Emergency managers, brigades, scientists and land managers get one record in one unit for historical analysis, research and planning, such as reviewing past seasons and the critical season of an area; it is not a real-time response tool.
  • Every month says how sure it is: observed, estimated or provisional, and pre-2012 estimates are labeled "indicative", so users can tell what the test supports from what may still be sensor change.
  • The test shows where harmonization works and where it does not: estimated levels with honest ranges, but unusual-month flags that still depend on the sensor.
  • Local cases built in: the Puebla/Popocatépetl area (Mexico), where a volcano is not a wildfire, and the Bahía Blanca area (Argentina).

Tools

  • Python (DuckDB, pandas, NumPy, SciPy, GeoPandas, Shapely, PyYAML, Matplotlib; PyArrow as the Parquet engine) for data, harmonization, validation and figures.
  • JavaScript in a static site: Leaflet (map), Leaflet.draw (area drawing), ECharts (calendar charts) and hyparquet (reads Parquet tiles in the browser for the CSV); exact versions, licenses and checksums in app/vendor/VERSIONS.md.
  • GitHub and GitHub Pages for code and hosting.
  • Claude Code (SI) for code and drafts; ElevenLabs (SI) for the demo voice; see "Use of SI".
  • Pre-existing development tools, written before the event with SI and declared: the "sakit" toolkit (analysis, evidence ledger), agent skills and document templates. The public product does not copy sakit; the functions it needs (the count-ratio baseline and the leakage audit) were rewritten in English during the event.

Next steps

  • Find out why unusual-month flags still depend on the sensor, starting from the count classes (in Argentina, the 30–100 detections-per-month class passed on its own); any such analysis is post-test and not pre-registered.
  • Add more regions with the same pipeline and their own calibration (full transfer between Mexico and Argentina failed in our test).
  • Add NOAA-21 once enough standard data overlap with the series.
  • Compare with burned-area products and link official ground statistics (no figures from them yet).
